I would ask the Prime Minister whether or not his attention has been called to the publication

of what purports to be a copy of the recent Waterways Treaty between His Majesty and the United States of America in the 'Evening Telegram' of Toronto; my attention has been directed to it in that newspaper. I do not know whether it has been published in any other. I do not know whether the terms of the treaty are correctly set forth, but if they are correctly set forth I would ask the Prime Minister whether or not there is any special reason why the treaty should not be laid upon the table of the House. It seems rather unnecessary to keep up the pretense of secrecy when this treaty, through some means, I do not know what, is being published in the press of the country. If it is being correctly published then there seems no reason why it should not be laid before parliament. If it is not being correctly published, I invite the attention of the Prime Minister to what purports to be an accurate copy of the treaty in terms, and I think it ought to be stated that that is not a correct copy of the treaty if the alleged publication is not founded upon fact. There would seem to be no good reason why the parliament of this country should be kept officially ignorant of the terms of the treaty when it is being published in the press of the United States and Canada and in the press of Great Britain, because a very full summary of it appeared in the London 'Times' of January 28 last.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have seen from time to time in the newspapers of this country reports which pretended to be copies of the Waterways Treaty. Some were fairly accurate and some were not so accurate. I have not seen the publication in the Toronto 'Telegram' to which my hon friend refers. If I understand him aright, the publication purports to be a verbatim copy of the treaty. It may or it may not
It purports to be a copy of the message of President Roosevelt to the Senate conveying to the Senate the terms of the treaty in absolutely accurate form.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that it is not, but if it is I am quite sure that it has not reached the public by the permission of the United States authorities. It may have come to the newspapers in some surreptitious manner. I can only say to my hon. friend that I quite agree with him and that I see no reason why the treaty should not be made public immediately.

If that committee is delayed the prorogation of the House will be delayed in order that certain business may be brought to a conclusion. I think it is very important, in the interest of an early prorogation, that we should have more frequent meetings of that committee and a word from the Prime Minister would mean a great deal towards the accomplishment of that very desirable object.

That in the opinion of this House, the appalling number of accidents at level crossings demand that the matter of railway crossings throughout the whole of Canada should at once engage the earnest consideration of the people's municipal and parliamentary representatives.
2.	This imminent, and increasing peril incident to the present method of railway construction and operation may, by slow degrees, and in isolated instances, be mitigated by the exercise of powers vested in the Railway Board, but can never reach the thousands and thousands of cases crying out for safeguards, and cannot reach even a tithe of them within any reasonable time.
3.	The question of railway crossings from ocean to ocean is a matter of supreme importance, and urgent to the last degree. The toll of sacrifice increases with the multiplications of lines and the increase of speed and traffic, and no sensible improvement can be hoped for so long as the initiative for redress is left to casual and individual action.
4.	The rule, and the presumption from the acceptance of a charter, should be separated, or protected crossings elsewhere, with the onus upon the company of establishing a justi-

fication for exceptional treatment in exceptional cases.
5.	It is the duty of the government early this session to deal with the whole question of railway crossings in a thorough and comprehensive way and with a view of eliminating, as far as reasonably possible, the level crossings from our system of railways, and where this cannot be done, the adoption of such other methods and devices as will secure, in as great a degree as is possible, the safety of the people using the highways.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move this resolution I realize that it is a very broad and a very difficult question, and that there are many members in the House who would present it in a more efficient way than I may be able to. I realize too-and I hope I shall be understood as expressing that opinion throughout, any argument I may use-the very important services rendered by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) upon one phase of the question, namely, as regards that portion of the railway crossings on highways in Canada situated within the limits of thickly settled portions of cities, towns, and villages. I shall on this occasion endeavour to enlist the sympathy and attention of the representatives of the people on the broad question of the elimination of railway crossings on the level of the highways as far as our circumstances and conditions will permit, having regard to the vast extent of our country and to the enormous expense involved in a complete separation of railway and highway grades. In presenting this motion I hone that I shall perhaps have the satisfaction of having it accepted by the government without opposition, and I may say that last year, of two resolutions which were so accepted by the government I had the honour of presenting one. I do not propose this resolution in any political sense, and consequently I trust that in its support I will have the united action of all members of the House. Last night I obtained a_ return as to the number of accidents on railway crossings during the last five years. That return does not give us complete information ; in fact the scar-citv of information and the delay in obtaining it is not exactly suggestive of energy in devising a remedy which will prevent these accidents. The Minister of Railways has recently indicated that this session he intends to take some action in the matter, and I give him my assurance that I will endeavour so far as I can to co-operate with him in securing the best possible solution of this question. The return of the accidents which have occurred at railway level crossings for the last five years ought to be sufficient to arouse the government to action and to cause them to follow the example of the government of the United States and of other countries in announcing a definite policy.
We have in Canada 15,000 level crossings. Of these it is said that 3,115 are already-protected. The nature of the protection has not been stated, and I think it is very important that we should know whether or not as a matter of fact we have that number of crossings actually and effectively protected. In perusing the returns I would be inclined to think not, for I find that a good many accidents have occurred at crossings said to be protected. Now, no sensible man will imagine that we can have all the railway crossings from one end of Canada to the other-15,000 at the present time, and more being constructed from year to year-made absolutely safe for the people using the highways. I realize that. 1 realize that there are thousands of crossings, on the western prairies and in other parts of the Dominion, where there is an open view of approaching trains from either side, and where the highway is also visible to those operating the trains-which require no artificial devices in order that people may be reasonably safe. On the other hand, I feel that there are hundreds, perhaps thousands, which should have some protection in the nature of a gate. There are highway crossings which, however sparsely settled the locality may be, may operate as a trap; for instance, where the railway is cut through an embankment, and where the highway approaches the railway through a cutting, so that a person passing along the highway cannot see an approaching train until it is almost upon him. All these should have protection of some kind, and I believe it will be found that they should be provided with gates. Then there are undoubtedly, not only in the crowded centres but also in the rural parts of the country, scores and perhaps hundreds of cases where, at a reasonable expenditure of money, the highways could be separated from the railway, being placed either above or below the railway.
The returns for five years show that in Canada during that time there have been 270 deaths at level crossings and 350 injuries, making a total of 620 casualties. The returns are from the Railway Board, the Intercolonial Railway and the Controller of Statistics in the Railway Department. It is a peculiar fact that in all the enormous number of crossings there are not a very great many where accidents have occurred, and there are some which have been great offenders. For instance, the Grimsby accident of the other day followed a great disaster of some time ago ; and a little precaution would have prevented both. Dunnville is in the same category. Last fall a Mrs. Miller and her child were run down by a train at this crossing, and perhaps a little precaution on our part would have prevented that accident. Kingston has been the scene of a good many accidents. There, on the 20th

March, 1905, a man was killed; on the 6th of October, 1906, a man was killed at Princess street; again, on the 19th of December, 1907, another person was killed at Montreal street. Toronto, too, has been in a condition which would have suggested a remedy for a long time. There a person was killed on the 16th of January, 1905; another on the 3rd of November, 1905; another on October 16, 1906; on January 7, 1907, one was severely injured; in March, 1907, a person was killed, and at another crossing a person was severely injured. That something should have been done is made plain by the fact that three of these accidents occurred at one crossing, namely, that at Brock avenue.
As I have said, we have not very detailed information in this matter, in connection
with the operation of our railways in Canada, hut we have important statistics with regard to a country very similar to ours, that is, the United States, and! a brief examination of the conditions there may be helpful to us in determining what we should do. In 1888 the State of Massachusetts took the lead and appointed a railway commission. The report of that commission brought out a somewhat startling fact, which has been further demonstrated and emphasized in recent years; that is, that a greater number of people are killed at railway crossings than there are of passengers killed on the trains. The report of the Massachusetts Commission showed that in 1890, of the total number of people killted, 7 per cent were passengers, 33 per cent employees, 47 per cent trespassers, stealing rides or walking along the railway track, &e., and 11 per cent were people killed at highway crossings. This fact is more than borne out by the statistics of the United States since that date. From 1900 to 1906 inclusive, the number of people killed at level crossings exceeded the total number of passengers killed on American railways by 85 per cent. Making the total number of victims at railway crossings, during those seven years, 12,971. Take the wonderful contrast we find where there is a separation of the railway from the highway. We have a striking instance of this in the case of the Columbian exhibition. Shortly before the exposition began, the Illinois Central Railway elevated some eight or nine miles of its tracks in Chicago. It did that at its own expense with the assistance of the Columbian exposition. Not a dollar was paid by the State or contributed by the city, although the expenditure was over $3,000,000. During the six months of that exhibition that railway company handled-largely by reason of having the streets and its railway lines separate-19,500,000 people without the loss of a single life. Other countries are doing something, and I ask my right horn friend ' what are you going to do about it.' That we ought to do something, I am sure he will admit. Mr. Borden D. Whiting, a railway commissioner on the New Jersey Board says:
Grade crossings must not be tolerated on crowded public thoroughfares and must be abolished before they are soaked in blood.
In my resolution I speak of ' imminent and increasing peril.' Why? Because the danger increases in proportion to the increasing number of trains and so on. And in the Dominion at present we are increasing in all those matters which go to make up danger. What is it that determines the number of accidents at level crossings? It is the number of trains and tracks, the speed of the trains, the character of the crossings and the extent of the highway traffic. Each one of these elements is an increasing quantity and contributes more and more to the danger as the years advance. I ask the Minister of Railways and the leader of the government what should be our great object in Canada to-day in connection with this railway question. We have had great railway problems to solve, but none so important as the one which now confronts us. Go into the library and you will find a dozen books upon the railway problem, and I venture to say that the heart of that problem for us is the protection of our highways and the providing of reasonable security for those who use them. Our object should be safety, in the first place, and then moderate tolls, speed, frequency of service and comfort. But the paramount object we should have in view is the public safety; and safety to the degree we hope to have it, cannot be obtained until we have grappled with this problem and endeavoured to solve it by eliminating grade crossings, wherever possible with reasonable expenditure; and, as an alternative, in all other cases where the crossings are concealed ot otherwise dangerous, by having gates and other devices for the public protection.

The ideal system is of course to be found in Great Britain. Britain was the first country to grasp the proper way of dealing with this question. In fact, I think I am right in saying that it is the only country which did realize at the outset the folly of sacrificing the highways in order to secure the railways. Germany has at present a magnificent railway system from the point of view of security and otherwise, second only perhaps to that of Great Britain. But the difference is this. Britain began right and preserved her highways while building her railways, whereas Germany sacrificed her highways to build her railways and then had to pay enormously in order to reclaim her highways and obtain the security for highway traffic which she now enjoys. But of course that security has only been obtained at an enormously increased cost and such will be the case in Canada, as it has been in the United States, when we come to reconstruct our system. In that regard we shall have to pay enormously more than we would have had to pay if we could have begun as Britain did.
Speaking on this question, I might say- and it is of interest now when we have the question of government ownership of railways coming up from time to time-that this subject is very closely connected with the question of the nationalization of railways. Germany has been enabled to separate the highways from the railways with greater facility by reason of the nationalization of her railways; and as a cognate proposition, just in proportion as we see to it that the companies afford a reasonable protection for all people having occasion to use the highways, shall we be postponing the day of the nationalization of railways in Canada.
Mr. Seth Low was speaking quite recently on the question of the Hepburn Bill. He pointed out that while the prediction had been made that that Bill would be a failure, one year's operation of it had shown that the vesting of larger powers in the Railway Commission in the United States, had been an eminent success, not only because the measure was operating well by reason of the machinery conferred upon the board, but because the railways had immediately volunteered to carry out the provisions of the Act so that the Board of Commissioners were under no necessity to take action against them. And no doubt whenever you frame adequate laws for the protection of the public, you will have those to whom these laws are to be applied volunteering to carry out the orders of the board without waiting for action to enforce the law. Therefore, we may be encouraged in Canada, if we can form a policy on this great question by the belief that it will not require to be enforced in many instances, by the Board of Railway Commissioners, but that the railway companies will be on the alert to carry out the provisions of the law.
I have referred to the English system, and I wish to read a clause or two of the English statute as being the most concise way of expressing exactly what the law is in Great Britain. I realize that in Canada we cannot expect, except in our cities and large towns, to carry out the English system in anything like its entirely for many long years to come; but there can be no good reason advanced why we should not begin to eliminate the grade crossings. The English statute says:
If a line of railway crosses any turnpike road or public highway, then, except where otherwise provided by the special Act, either such road shall be carried over the railway or the railway shall be carried over such road by means of a bridge, and such bridge with the immediate approaches and all other necessary works connected therewith, shall be executed and at all times thereafter maintained at the expense of the company.
Provided always, that with the consent of two or more justices in petty sessions, as after mentioned, it shall be lawful for the company to carry the railway across any highway, other than a public carriage road, on the level.
Now, we have this condition of things that, even with the enormous railway system in Great Britain, there can be no level crossing, except by special Act of_ parliament, upon any road where driving is done.
The next section provides for the maintenance of gates where the railway crosses a carriage road on the level, which gates are to be kept closed except when in actual use by persons crossing the railway-the exact opposite of what we adopt in Canada, though I am not prepared to say which is the better of the two-and providing that there shall be men in attendance, as we have here. But the lowest order of protection in Great Britain, from one end of it to the other, is gates, with a house in which a man is to be lodged and the other appliances for the safety of the public, such as devices for lighting, the ringing of bells and other means of helping to safeguard the public.
Now, it should be distinctly understood, also, that every dollar of the expense of these works in Great Britain is borne by the railways. In saying that, I do not want to be unreasonable. We have to recognize that the railways are a great factor in the development of Canada. I do not want to be a crank and say we can do the same here as is done in Great Britain. All I say is that the fact is as I have stated, and it is a fact that should be kept in mind as one of the elements in the case. There is another provision in the law of Great Britain, and if we had had that here the Grimsby disaster could not have occurred. It is as follows:

Coming to the next great railway country, France, I shall read a clause from their law.
Except in the case of local obstacles sufficiently serious in the opinion of the government, any railway intersecting national highways or depari nu*ntal roads shall pass above or below such highways or roads.
A gentleman dealing with this says:
Level crossings are tolerated only on rural or private cross-roads.
I find on .further research that when a railway passes a highway or public path on a level it must have a gate of specified style, it must have a man in attendance; a cottage is provided at an expense ordinarily of $1,000 and all the expense entailed is borne by the railway company. In that connection we must not lose sight of the fact that in France not only is all the expense borne by the railway companies but the railways revert to the state after a period of ninety-nine years.
To speak briefly of the conditions in the United States, I want the government to follow me in this idea. The governments of many states in the United States have adopted the principle of defining what shall be the prevailing conditions in reference to the construction of railways over highways and this has also been, as you have perceived, the policy of Great Britain, Germany and France, and I think of European countries generally. Be that as it may, the

closest analogy you can get to our conditions is in the United States and they have adopted a definite policy as regards the features of railway construction which I am now discussing. I want to urge upon the government that they should and should now at this session enunciate the policy that we shall have, as far as possible, as to the existing roads a separation of the highway from the railway, that we shall in other cases wherever necessary have a protection by gate or other properly approved device, that that shall be the policy of the law of the country and that its working out only shall be left to the railway board.
. Massachusetts I think was the first state in the field. Their law provides that there shall be no new railway constructed on a grade crossing until the board has investigated the matter and has ordered that it may be so
Then as to the existing roads, the general law provides the policy that shall be adopted for reclaiming the highways by separation of the highway from the railway. The general law is that the railway pays 65 per cent, the state pays 25 per cent or more and the municipality pays 10 per cent or less. That is to say there is 35 per cent of the cost to be borne between the municipality and the state and the board may order any proportion of that 35 per cent to be paid by the state, but cannot order the municipalities to pay more than 10 per cent. Expenditure by the state is limited to $500,000 in any one year and to $5,000,000 in all. Then they have special statutes by which they eliminated a great number of grade crossings at certain points, notably Boston, Brocton and Newton. In reference to these cities the state paid 31| per cent, the cities 135 per cent and the company 55 per cent.
New York attempted to adopt the Massachusetts law with regard to the expenditure. The railways were not exactly opposed to the abolition of the grade crossing in the state but they were opposed to the allotted proportion of the expense. Let me say that I do not understand that the railways will put up any organized hostility to the proposition that we are making but may object to the proportion of the expense they are to pay. The railways realize that in the interests of the traffic which they wish to handle, the desire for rapidity, the desire for safety and the elimination of that, much vexed question of the cattle guard in many instances, it is to their interest as much as possible to separate the highway from the railway crossing, and to have protection at other points. New York therefore was not able by reason of the strong organized opposition of the big railway interests to pass a law as favourable to the people as the Massachusetts law, and the law there is that the company shall pay 50 per cent, the state 25 per cent and the municipality 25 per cent. Their law provides:
All steam surface railroads, hereafter built except additional switches and sidings, must be so constructed as to avoid all public crossings at grade, wherever practicable so to do.
And as regards the division of expense:
Whenever under the provisions of section
60	of this Act new railroads are constructed across existing highways, the expense of crossing above or below the grade of the highway shall be paid entirely by the railroad corporations.
It then goes on to provide for conditions such as the extension of a new street where none before existed, across an existing railway.
Mr, GRAHAM. Where the railway has possession of the territory first does it make any difference as to the cost ?

Yes, it does. The section reads:
Whenever, under the provisions of section
61	of this Act a new street, avenue or highway is constructed across an existing railroad, the railroad corporation shall pay one half and the municipal corporation wherein such street, avenue or highway is located shall pay the remaining one-lialf of the expense of making such crossing, above or below grade; and whenever a change is made as to an existing crossing, in accordance with the provisions of section 62 of this Act, 50 percentum of the expense thereof shall be borne by the railroad corporation, 25 per cent by the municipal corporation and 25 per cent by the state.
In the case of a new railway the railway pays the whole of it; if it is the change of an existing grade, where the highway was in possession first then the railway pays 50 per cent, the state 25 per cent, and the municipality 25 per cent. In Maine they have practically the Massachusetts law where they want to change the grade with regard to an existing highway and an existing railway. Then, the statute provides that for a new railway there shall be a separation of grade unless the Railway Commissioners, after notice, authorize the crossing on the level, the elimination of level crossings being the rule, the cost being borne entirely, I think, by the company, although, as to that, I am not positive. The state of Michigan has pretty drastic laws as to this question. It puts it into_ the power of the Board of Railway Commissioners to order whatever they like as regards the protection of railway crossings. The elimination of level crossings, the separation of grades, the providing of gates, the providing of flagmen or whatever thev think necessary they can order if they think fit and the entire cost is charged to the railway company. In Ohio the company pays 65 ner cent, or more if so ordered.
Who pays the balance in Ohio?

The balance is paid either by the state or by the municipality; I am inclined to think that it is the state that pays the 35 per cent. As regards Connecticut, the commissioner may order of his own motion the separation of grades. In that case the company pays 75 per cent, and the state pays 25 per cent. Then, there may be the case of the application by a railway company for the elimination of a grade crossing. In that case the company pays the entire cost and, in that connection, I may say that they are bound by statute to apply for the elimination of one level crossing every year. Each company must apply for the elimination of at least one level crossing each year for every sixty miles of their railway, and the result has been that in ten years they have cut out 549 level crossings out of a total of 1,526, leaving 977 to be provided for in the state. They have also a provision as to the case where the application is by the municipality and where the railway existed before it was crossed by the highway. Then, as to new railways to be constructed after the passing of the Act, they are to have separate grades constructed at the cost of the company. There are other states, many of which have been referred to in the public press, and it is not necessary for me to deal with further illustrations. They enunciate clearly enough the policy of the United States with regard to this matter. They show clearly that they have come to the conclusion that it is not wise to leave it entirely to the Railway Board, but that the representatives of the people should define, within general limits, what shall be the policy as to this great and important matter.
As to the question of cost, that is, of course, a matter for the government to consider, but they are always anxious to have some idea from us so that they shall not go wrong. I have clear ideas as to some portions of this question and not very clear ideas as to others, but I would like to give the government the benefit of my consideration as far as it has gone. How are we to meet the expense? As to new roads, as to any charter that we shall grant during this session, I submit to the government that we should make it the law that the railway company shall separate the highway from the railway, or that they shall provide gates as a good alternative, unless they show that in particular instances the separation or the gates are not necessary, and (fliat they should pay the entire cost of the work. I would recommend that policy with reference to all new railways, unless, having regard to any peculiar local conditions, such as the extending of the railway through a sparsely settled portion of Canada, we should, for good reasons, see fit to exempt them from that liability by the statute by what they shall be chartered. As to the question of municipalities contributing towards the expense, I shall leave to the city municipali-Mr. LANCASTER.
ties the fighting out of that question for themselves, but as to the rural municipalities I do not feel that there should be no portion of the expense charged up to them.	I might interject just
here, with great respect to the Railway Board, that I am sorry that in the matter of the Grimsby crossing, they did not observe that rule. I claim that in every case where the highway and railway cross upon the level and where the highway was one of the original highways which existed at the time the railway was built, the company should be at the total charge of providing and maintaining all the appliances for safety that may be ordered by the railway board. As to the further question of expense as to existing roads that we have to deal with, that are in existence to-day, reclaiming our highways in that regard, I do not feel that perhaps I am very competent to pronounce a judgment upon that, but as I feel at present, I do not think it would be unreasonable that Canada should contribute something to the expense. The railwavs helped to make Canada. It was absolutely impossible at the time some of these roads were built that the precautions which were taken in Great Britain and the older countries of Europe could be taken here, and T say that to put these railways upon a proper basis as regards these crossings, it does not appear at the present time to be unreasonable that the Dominion government should contribute something towards the change of grade. As to the sources of income available to the country there is this point to be kept in mind by the government and by parliament in dealing with this question: England taxes her railways to the extent of $1,000 a mile and the United States tax theirs to an enormous extent. We nominally are beginning to tax ours through the provinces. This tax is very little and I would not be sorry if I could see an arrangement made between the Dominion and the provinces by which the provinces would forego tbe taxing of railways if the money were diverted to securing a better condition of things as regards railway crossings. In the United States the lowest amount at which any railway was taxed in 1906 in an organized state was $107 per mile, and the highest was $1,683 per mile, an average of $349 per mile ifor all the railways in the United States. Pennsylvania alone paid in 1906, as railway taxation, $6,982,973. The United States collected from all the railways in that year $74,602,171. If Canada collected on her railways at the same rate at which they impose taxes on railways in the United States, a revenue of from $8,000,000 to $9,000,000 a year would be obtained.
Do you know what the federal taxes on the United States railways amount to?

I have not got that separately. I was suggesting to the govern-

ment that probably some adjustment should be made in reference to the taxation, which obtains in Canada now whereby the burden upon the railways in changing grades would be lightened. It should be borne in mind too, that we have contributed very largely towards railway building, at a much higher rate than the United States have. The United States never have a cash subsidy to a railway and they have not given a land grant since 1871. Mr. Blaine estimates that the total contribution to railway building in the United States by the various municipalities and governments amounted all told to $1,000,000,000, and had they aided railways as liberally as we in Canada have it would amount to three or four billions, instead of one.
Is there any federal taxation on railways in the United States?
I should judge from what I was reading that there was, but I did not ascertain the amount.
Then there would be federal, and state, and municipal taxation on the railways of the United States.

Yes. I am merely suggesting that we are taxing our railways very little in the first place, and in the second place that probably some distribution could be made in the line of diverting existing taxation to this very desirable work. In conclusion, I may say I have every hope that at last-not much beh'nd the rest of us, but a little behind the rest of us-the government has come to realize the importance of this subject. I am not too sanguine as to what the government may do. Some things would indicate that they are not prepared to do much just at present. It does not look as if the government had considered the question for any length of time; we had no indication of it in the speech from the Throne; we had a very hesitating acceptance of the Lancaster Bill, but we have got it and I hope the government has put the Senate into proper order with regard to it.
What, what?

We had no data a month ago and what is now brought down after a month of delay is very meagre. There was a hurry up order by the Minister of Railways a little while ago upon the railway board and there was a response, but that response has not been divulged to us. There was another hurry up order on the board when the Lancaster Bill came on, but that I understand, was not responded to.
Would my hon. friend tell me what that was?

When the Lancaster Bill came up for third reading, I understood the minister to say that he had written to
the chairman of the railway board, that he expected an answer from him, and that he would like the matter to stand over. I do not say, however, that it concludes the matter that there was no response to that hurry up order.
That is a stretch of imagination.

I only mean to show that the Minister of Railways has awakened to the necessity of there being some protection. He did not think of it until we brought it to his attention, but that is no reflection on him if he does the right thing now. Of course it is for the government to formulate their own policy, but I would suggest to the right hon. the leader of the government that on this question it would be wise to consult the municipal representatives of the people, and I would like to see him bring to Ottawa representatives from all the county councils and municipal councils, and as it is a matter for the general advantage of Canada and for the general advantage of the railway companies and for the unbounded advantage of our people, I would like to see them get the railway companies to transport these gentlemen free of charge to Ottawa. If he did that he would have the benefit of the advice and suggestions of the immediate representatives of the people. I would also urge the great necessity for getting information upon the subject. We know the number of railway crossings there are in Canada, but that is about all we do know. With all respect for the railway board, I believe it is impossible for them to grapple with this question, unless they have greater assistance than they yet have. I believe the first thing to do is to employ competent men to collect material throughout the country and to bring in a general report as to the condition of all railway crossings in Canada, classifying them and saying: at this point the crossings require no protection, at this point certain protection is required and at this point the level crossing shall be abolished. Let the railway companies be heard and let the people locally interested be heard and let a determination be come to as to what remedy shall be adopted in respect to existing railways. I also urge upon the governemnt that they should make a declaration of policy upon this matter and that there should be a law made by parliament to guide us. It is not enough that we have six competent members of the railway board; we have a parliament here of more than 200 members and it is the wisdom of parliament, centered if you like in the government, that should pronounce upon the policy of Canada in this matter. We have been drifting along and in a little while we will have our court made law made by the railway board. I am here to say that I do not think it is wise that we should have that condition of things. It is

for the courts to construe the law and to enforce it, not to make it, and I do not distinguish between the railway board and other courts in that regard. What I suggest is that we should adopt a Canadian policy declaring that all the King's highways shall be safe-I mean reasonably safe, not absolutely safe, but relatively safe-that in future railway construction the safety of the highways should be guarded and that a remedy shall be applied where safety under existing conditions is absent.
Then, as I have said, and as the resolution more concisely indicates, the presumption should be protection everywhere- that every railway company shall prima facie be bound to protect the interests of those who cross the railway on the high-wav, and in order to be exonerated in any particular case, it must show the railway board that there is needed either no protection or only a certain kind of protection.
These views are very inadequately expressed, I know. I feel that this is a very difficult but at the same time an engrossing and all-important matter. I know that 1 have had the very complimentary close attention of the right hon. leader of the government during my imperfect discussion of this matter, and for that I am exceedingly grateful. I recognize just as fully as anybody that the desire of protecting the people does not belong only to one side of the House; I recognize that we are all at one in the desire to do what is in the best interests of the country. But I have urged this matter to some extent also from a knowledge that railway companies have powerful influence, and that they exert this powerful influence upon the government benches, as they will endeavour, I suppose, to exert them upou us at no distant date. And so I have at some length ventured to urge very strongly my views on the government. May I put the matter in another form? I think our primary law should be that the highway and the railway crossing should be separate, the one above the other; that our secondary law should be that where that condition cannot obtain, there shall be the protection of a gate wherever there is anything in the nature of a trap or shut-in crossing and that the railway company can always escape an undue burden bv showing to the railway board that in the particular instance referred to the need of safeguards does not exist. In that way we shall have what will be fair to the people, and, what is of equal importance, just to the railway company.
In concluding, let me refer to what has been said across the floor of the House, on one occasion at least. Some gentleman on this side of the House said to the distinguished leader of the government that he had had some rare opportunities of distinguishing himself during the time of his ad-Mr. LENNOX.
ministration. The right hon. gentleman admitted that he had had some opportunities of distinguishing himself in regard to the great problems that confront us from time to time in this House. Whilst he has had many such opportunities in the past, he has had no better opportunity of distinguishing himself than he has now in dealing, in a large, broad, comprehensive, statesmanlike way, with this great and im-: minent problem now confronting us. He has not only an opportunity of distinguishing himself, but what is far better, an opportunity which I hope he will embrace, of doing lasting good to the people of Canada in the solution of this great question.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the House has listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of my hon. friend. They have shown that he has paid a good deal of attention to this question and has devoted considerable research to ascertaining the conditions that exist in other countries. I may say in the outset, that I think there is not much difference of opinion between us as to the end we all desire to attain. Possibly later on there may appear to be not much difference as to the means necessary for attaining that desired end. My hon. friend, of course, with his usual sense of humour, could not refrain from interjecting a joke concerning what he called my hurry-up order; but he did it with such good nature and so obviously with his usual humourous intent, that i forgive him.
He knew you would appreciate the joke.

Yes. I am glad to see that the question of the Railway Commission is one on which there is no difference of opinion. We agree that they have done good work, are doing good work, and will probably do good work where we give them that work to perform. This question of railway crossings opens up the great question of transportation in one or two aspects. We must concede that unless Canada's trade is to stand still and she is to be outstripped in the matter of transportation, fast trains must be run, and run daily, both for passengers and freight. For years we have tried to attain that object; because it must be remembered that in this country the public carriers have not the advantages that they have either in the old land or in the United States. As I have said time and again, it is the density of population that makes traffic. Some of the states referred to by my hon. friend have so much greater traffic than we have in this part ot the world, that the conditions are not similar in so far as the burdens carried by the railways are concerned. I admit with him that the conditions in the old land-in Great Biitain, Germany and France-are ideal

i
conditions. But if he will compare those countries with Canada in regard to density of population, he will see that Canada cannot be compared with them as to the conditions of transportation. Canada is a new country, and it has been our endeavour, both m Dominion, provincial and municipal boundaries, to encourage the improvement of transportation facilities. It may he possible that we have carried this encouragement to a larger extent in all these spheres than some at this date may think we should have done. But we were dealing with the transportation problem in its earlier stages, and I believe the people of Canada,, the people of the provinces and the residents of municipalities would under similar conditions do the same thing again for the improvement of transportation. Now, as I have said, these fast trains must be run. The question of income to the people who work on the farm and in the factory is largely tied up with the transportation problem. The prices they are to obtain depend not wholly on the quantity or quality of the goods they produce. They might produce goods in large quantities or of excellent quality; but unless transportation facilities were, provided to get their goods to the markets of the world quickly and in good condition, they might as well not have produced at all or in as great quantities or of such excellent quality. The price of the goods depends on the quality that exists when they reach the market, and that quality sometimes depends on the speed with which they are taken to market. Now, in whatever is don" or decided to be done in Canada, this must be borne in mind, that the interests of the people and the interests of the railways are one in the matter of bringing the producer as closely as possible to the consumer, or, in other words, to the markets of the world. In Great Britain the conditions are ideal. As my hon. friend has pointed out, in the construction of their railways they provided against level crossings. But, as I have said before, the conditions, even in the construction of these roads, perhaps were not as ours are.
My hon. friend mentions another thing which I think worthy of note. He said that the United States have not in recent years given any aid to railways. That is true, I believe. But this must be remembered in making a comparison between the two countries. The United States had no rival practically in the development of their trade, so far as this continent was concerned, whereas Canada has to build up a commercial position and develop her trade side by side and in competition with a country like the United States whose population is ten times greater than ours. It is like building a main street through a great many of our towns^ and villages. Scattered along it on both sides are inhabited and vacant
lots, but the village or town is not compact, and it costs large amounts of money m many of our municipalities to build such streets and sidewalks which necessarily extend over a large territory. That is exactly the condition in Canada. We have a territory as large as the United States, but a population twelve times smaller. If we had not given any aid to our railways, we would not to-day have the Canada we have. Canada has taken the position she enjoys in the markets of the world because people have been safe in going to any part of our new country in the hope that within a reasonable time they would be furnished with railway facilities to carry their products to market. That has been the principle which has guided the governments of Canada and the provinces and our municipal councils in giving aid to railways.
My hon. friend pointed out that the conditions of the crossings should be examined into. That is true, but in his own remarks lie gave us a fairly accurate answer. He said that, in the experience of the last five years-which is the best experience we can have as it brings us through .the -time when we have had the most rapid transportation-the dangerous crossings in Canada have been practically located and have been confined to a comparatively few localities. Of course I would not pretend to say that there are no dangerous crossings where no one has been killed, but the more dangerous ones would naturally be where accidents have taken place. Some two years ago the Board of Railway Commissioners proceeded to ascertain the location of the various crossings in the Dominion and asked the railway companies to give them schedules or plans of these crossings. There are a great many of these plans in the possession of the board at present and others are constantly coming. Of course, it is a little difficult for the Railway Commissioners, with the engineering staff at their command, to get them all in the order and condition they want, but they are getting them as rapidly as possible. I did urge the board a few weeks ago to make an examination of the dangerous crossings so that we could have some reliable data, and a return has been brought down which gives us a pretty good idea of these crossings and their results. I find, in looking over the return, that there were killed in Canada during the last five years 270 people at ievel crossings. That is a loss of life which is deplorable, though, I admit, not as large as I thought it would be when I asked for the information. My hon. friend quoted one railway on which no loss of life occurred last year at level crossings.
I might say to him-and it may be something in favour of government management of railways-that on Prince Edward Island no fatal level crossing accident has taken

place during the last five years. On the Intercolonial Railway, during the last five years, fifteen fatal accidents have occurred at level crossings, but this may be incidental to the country and location, because, of course, all level crossings are not dangerous.
I now come to a difficulty which does not confront any state in the union in dealing with this question. In Canada as in the United States we have our federal authorities and we have our provincial authorities as they have their state authorities, and we each have our municipal authorities. In the United States the railways are largely under the control of the state unlike Canada where they are under the control of the federal authorities. If my hon. friend will study the question of railway commissions in the United States he will find that the states have_ boards of their own in most cases, while in Canada we have the one board which controls the whole country. A state legislature can say what a municipality must do. These legislatures control the highways^ through the municipalities, but the Dominion of Canada cannot say what a municipality must do, speaking in general terms, as it does not control the municipality and it does not control the highways, the highways being under the control of the municipalities, and the municipalities in their turn being governed by the provincial authorities. So that it is easier for the state authorities to deal with the whole question, municipal and provincial, than it is for the Dominion. And my hon. friend will have noticed that in the division of expenditure, it was not between the United States federal authorities, the municipalities and the railways, but between the state legislatures, the municipalities and the railways. There is that difference, but it is not insurmountable, and I am prepared to say now that while it is more difficult to work out in Canada than in any state in the union, still the difficulties are not such that we need despair of being able to overcome them.
Did not the Board of Railway Commissioners make a division of the expenditure in connection with the proposed viaduct in Toronto?
And Grimsby?
That is a level crossing.
There must be some way of working that out.

I think the distinction is this, that where the municipality has asked to have it done, then the board can impose part of the burden on the municipality, but under the state jurisdiction, the board can impose it no matter who asks. And in the city of Toronto, I think that the

city itself asked the board to make a ruling. At Kingston the board did make a ruling, imposing part of the expenditure on the county, part on the county and part on the railway, but that was done at the request of the county if I remember rightly.
They make an agreement previously, I think, and that agreement is carried out by an order of the Railway Commission.
I think at Kingston there was an order of the board on the application of the county.
I think the hon. gentleman is right. Where the municipality makes an application the Railway Commission may grant the application subject to conditions.

Our statute does not say it is a condition precedent that the municipality must make the application. The jurisdiction is general. Under sections 237, 238, 239 the board may act on its own motion without application from any municipality.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Will my hon. friend read the section?

Section 237, subsection
2:
The board may, by order, grant such application upon such terms and conditions as to protection, safety and convenience of the public, as it may deem expedient or may order that the highways be carried over or under the railway, or be temporarily or permanently diverted, and that such works be executed, watchmen or other persons employed, or measures taken as under the circumstances appear to the board best adapted to remove or diminish the danger or obstruction arising or likely to arise therefrom.
That is where the railway is originally being constructed. Then comes section 238:
Where the railway is already constructed upon, along or across any highway the board may order the company within a specified time to submit to the board a plan and profile of such portion of the railway, and may upon such submission, make any order in respect thereof, as in the last preceding section provided.
If the board can make an order under section 237, making it impossible for the company to have a level crossing, surely they can, under section 238, order a company already existing to take away its level crossing?

I am not sure that that touches the point. They can make the order, but that does not apportion the expense. All the orders, whatever the powers, have been made under the conditions stated. I may be wrong, but that is my recollection. The question has been raised

how far the jurisdiction of the board can extend over a municipality. There is the principle of law which, roughly stated, is that, where parliament has the right to pass a certain Act, it can pass any other law in order to enforce the original one, even if the second Act is not altogether within its jurisdiction. In that relation it has been held that they could impose the amount of costs or even a penalty on the municipality. However the difficulty then arises, as the hon. member will understand, that we in this Dominion parliament have not the control of the municipalities as the states have to which he is referring. But, as I said a moment ago', that does not mean an insuperable difficulty. If there is to be a comprehensive measure dealing with level crossings in a satisfactory way, it cannot be attained by doing anything to make a division among the people, either as to municipalities, provinces or in any other way. We must agree to some measure which, while it may impose burdens that otherwise would not be imposed, will be in accordance with the conditions which exist in Canada. It is a difficult problem to work out. I have spent not minutes, but hours and days in trying to solve it. and have come across difficulties too numerous to be detailed to the House. It is a large problem, and' yet has many small details which are difficult to work out. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) touched one. I think, perhaps, he is wrong; but he has touched this side of the question, which, no doubt, is a popular one to touch but mav not be practicable in working out the question that no rural municipality should be asked to pay. He leaves the cities to fight out their own battles. I am afraid we should not succeed if we approached the question in that way. If we are to eradicate the danger of level crossings, somebody must bear some burden: and the people who have helped to create the condition, no matter who they may be, will have to be asked to bear a reasonable share of the burden of removing the condition which they themselves have helped to create. How far that principle ought to be carried I do not know. But let me point out-and I would call my hon. friend's special attention to this point- that in every state he mentioned the principle which he said he would not adopt has been adopted. That is, the municipalities have to pay a share, though a minor share, of the expense.
Many, but not all.

My hon. friend is quoting these states as examples for us to follow, but drawing a line at that point. Perhaps he is right. But I submit that if we are going to make a success of getting rid of the level crossings, we must not say anything that would create lack of harmony, and we must all be ready to bear a fair
share of the burden that must be borne in order to bring about the result. We have all contributed to bring about the present condition. My hon. friend pointed out that a new provision is laid down for railways yet to be built. That is quite true. The Dominion has contributed to the conditions which now exists because, for years and years, we have allowed railways to be built under charters granted wthout any great restraint as to how their crossings should be constructed, or even how their entrance into cities should be made. Of recent years, and as the traffic has grown greater and railways have become the more numerous, the conditions under which railways are to be constructed are made more stringent, and greater care is taken than was thought necessary years ago. I submit that the provinces have contributed their share as to the present conditions. Not a few of the railways now under federal jurisdiction received their charters and powers of construction, and were actually constructed, under provincial authority. 'Some of them are still under provincial control, though comparatively few. I believe I am not putting it too strongly when I say that all railways doing more than a merely local business would better serve the people, and be better controlled, under our jurisdiction. However that may be, the provinces, in granting these charters and allowing the construction of railways under their jurisdiction have assisted in bringing about present conditions in relation to grade crossings. The municipalities have also contributed. I have belonged to at least one municipal council, and have travelled a good deal throughout the province, and am aware that in years gone bv, every municipality that was asked to contribute a bonus, even for the shadow of a railway, was ready to give it. They do not grant these bonuses to the same extent now. But, in years gone by, they have allowed railways to cross even their main thoroughfares on the level and to run through the busiest parts of their towns without let or hindrance. This applies not only to rural municipalities, but also to towns and even cities. So, these conditions have been allowed to arise with the consent of us all, and I submit that we are all more or less bound, if we are going to make a success of the undertaking, to contribute, though possibly in a very small amount, to do something to get . rid of this difficulty which we have helped to create, and in the removal of which we are so deeply interested. The Dominion might grant aid, and the provinces might grant aid. And let me call my hon. friend's attention to another point, which, perhaps, will come up later on, and which is worthy of consideration. Presuming that the board has jurisdiction to fix the amount to be paid by a municipality, how is the municipality to raise the money? Speaking of the pro-

1216
vince of Ontario, it could not, under the provincial laws, pay that money without submitting a by-law to the people.
Or getting provincial legislation. .

I am coming to that. They must submit it to the people, or else go to the legislature for a special Act. This brings me back to the idea I have expressed, that, in order to make this a success, it will be necessary for all parties concerned to take concerted action. First, the Dominion ought to consider well what it should do . in this case. We cannot say what any province will do, but in order to be successful the federal authority ought to communicate with the various provinces with an idea of coming to some amicable arrangement by which they would assist, so far as possible, and pass legislation that would enable the municipalities to do their share if they were asked to under an order of the board.
No one would reasonably argue that the great share of this cost should not be borne by the railways themselves. Whatever division might be made among the rest of us would be a minor division. I would not like to enact that the state, municipality or province should be compelled to pay up to a certain limit; there might be cases where they should not pay up to the limit fixed, and if I were drafting a law to-morrow I would ask that they should not be called upon to pay more than a certain amount and it would be in the jurisdiction of the board whether they should pay a less amount or pay anything.
Looking at the accidents that have taken place during the last five years and the reports that have been given of those accidents at level crossings by the officials of the Board of Railway Commissioners, this peculiar fact stares us in the face, that if ordinary care had been exercised by the traveller on the highway, 90 per cent of these accidents would not have taken place.
Where do you get the evidence of that? That is the statement of the railways.
No, it is the statement of the officials handed to me by the Board of Railway Commissioners.
They get their information from the railways, the railways are the real authorities for that statement.

I think that is not correct. * Every accident that has occurred since the board was appointed has been investigated by an officer for that purpose and his report goes to the board and on these reports, I understand, this information has been furnished to me.
That I suppose is a very small proportion.
I think that wherever an accident takes place they send an officer to investigate the cause of the accident.
I think the report shows only 180 of that class out of a total of 270. There are a great many of which no particulars are given.
I repeat the statement that from the information I get I think 90 per cent of the accidents would not have occurred if the travellers had exercised due care.
Does that make any difference?

It possibly may not, but my hon. friend will understand its bearing when I complete my statement. It may not and does not alter the fact that if the railway crossings had not been there the accidents would not have taken place, nor does it alter the other fact that governments and parliaments have to keen in mind that the public often have to be protected against their own carelessness. This is a case where all are united in agreeing to protect the public against what may be their carelessness, but I submit to the judgment of the House that where the public are to be protected against accidents by public enactment, they ought to be asked to do something to help themselves. I refer my hon. friend to a law or to a practice that has become law through judgment of the courts, in Pennsylvania, that every traveller upon a public highway must stop before he crosses a railway track. A sign is placed at each crossing reading:
' Stop, look, listen.' The railway is compelled to put that sign at every crossing and the public are compelled to stop and read that warning or forfeit any claim to damages if they are injured; but I think the onus of proving that they did not obey that injunction is cast on the railway and my hoii. friend will agree that it is difficult for a railway to prove such a thing so that any burden put upon the people is offset by the onus being placed on the railway. If something could be placed in the law or the regulations which would infuse into the minds of the people obedience to such a mandate, if it did not compel obedience, that they ought for their own safety to stop before approaching a railway crossing, eight out of ten of the fatal accidents would never occur and the danger of level crossings would be reduced to a minimum. You ask how to do that-I do not know. I am not prepared to say and we might come to the point that this parliament had no jurisdiction, that we might be guilty of an interference, as lawyers say. with the civil rights of the individual, if we endeavoured to interfere and say how the individual was to travel along the highway when the highway belongs to the municipality and can only

be regulated by the municipality or the legislature.
In order to make this successful we must have the co-operation of all classes interested. I may frankly say to my hon. friend that I have not been idle on this question, I have been studying it with all the care I could exercise during a busy session and for some months before, and I am impressed as thoroughly as any man in the House can be impressed with the idea that it is time we had some systematic effort to protect, as far as possible, the lives of the people on the highways crossing the railways. It is not a question that can be settled off-hand or in a moment. I am free to take my hon. friend and the House into my confidence and say that I intend to bring this matter to the consideration of my colleagues in a very few days. I might go further and say that but for the absence of the Minister of Finance, I would have discussed it weeks ago. I have been holding it in abeyance in order that there might be a full discussion on it, and I have a policy in mind concerning it which I wish to lay before my colleagues. That having been said and with the full understanding that we are all in sympathy with the idea of eradicating as far as possible the level crossings, I know that my hon. friend will be satisfied not to press his motion until we have discussed it further. The conditions now existing as to railways that we may have helped to create may not have been our fault, but the conditions on railways hereafter created will be our fault. If we allow them to be built as they have been in the past. I take it for granted that this House would be prepared to support a measure which would in principle say that on any railways to be in future chartered by this House, except in the case of extensions for switches, terminals or something of that kind, the greatest care should be taken to avoid this danger. If, when these railways are constructed, it should be found by the Railway Commissioners that level crossings have to be removed or protected in any way the railways should be required, in that case, to bear all the burden of such removal or protection. They would then know what was before them when they construct a railway. They would have it constantly in their minds that if they did not protect these crossings when they were constructing the railway they would only have to go to the expense of protecting them a little later on and that no municipality, province or Dominion would help them. I have detained the House longer than I had any desire to do, but this is a pretty broad question, a question with regard to which we are all of one mind, a question to which there is no political or party side and one in regard to which it ought to be the endeavour of the House to come to some arrangement by which the lives of the people may be protected, and 39
even if in working out that scheme we may not all have our ideas carried out to the fullest extent, I believe the people of Canada will expect parliament to do something in order to bring about the desired result.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apprehend that the House will not find fault with me for saying a few words upon this important matter. I wish to thank the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) for the valuable statistics he has placed upon 'Hansard' for our information and the information of the whole country in dealing with this question. So far as the object to be served and so far as some of the principles involved in the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) are concerned, in the main I agree with him. But, as to the manner of working out these principles I must diHer to some extent and possibly if, for a few moments, I were to state frankly why I differ from some of the obseravtions of the Minister of Railways and Canals the time may not be entirely wasted. First of all, I would say that we must divide this subject into two subclasses. The elimination of level crossings is one thing, and requiring protection on level crossings is another thing entirely. In so far as the ideal and much hoped for condition of the elimination entirely of level crossings is concerned, I would say, from the knowledge of the subject that I have acquired, that it would not be an unreasonable thing that the state should pay a proportion of the expense. As far as allowing railways to still run upon the highways is concerned, and protecting the crossings because of the rapidly increasing danger, I would say, and I will give a few reasons for my belief, that the whole burden of that should be borne by the railways. The elimination is a condition where you are taking away from the railways something which you permitted them to suppose they had a right to in their charter. In the anxiety to build railways we permitted them to cross highways upon the level. I do not say that we usurped the right of the provinces, but if my hon. friend (the Minister of Railways and Canals) is right in saying that the provinces still control the highways, then we did usurp the jurisdiction of the provinces in so far as we permitted the railways to run across the highways, but we did it in the interest of building railways. We did it because otherwise the expense of building railways would have been prohibitive and we would not have had the transportation facilities in the country that we so much desired. When we permitted a railway to run upon or across a highway we gave it an easement- I do not say a right, but I do



say that their rights in regard to that matter are very much exaggerated. We gave them that permission for the sole purpose of securing the building of a railway outside of the provincial jurisdiction, and that railway, of course, became a work for the general advantage of Canada. It established a connection between one province and another, between one part of Canada and another, and became a national railway in that sense. As far as it was necessary for them to cross highways, we gave then that jurisdiction because otherwise we would not have had power to allow them to cross highways at all. In giving them that jurisdiction we were permitting them, for their own profit, and to encourage them to invest in the hope of the profit they would get, but still for their own profit, to use the King's highway for the purpose of their track, for the purpose of transporting from one part of the country to another. We must not forget also that we must look at the conditions which existed when we gave that easement or right; that is to say that the railways ran not one-half as fast as they run now, that they ran upon a single track and that the number of trains was probably 25 per cent of what it is now. People did not contemplate that within a few years the danger would be very much multiplied, as it has been by their running upon or across the highways in that way. It is only fair when we speak of our having contributed to the condition of danger upon the level crossing to say that when we gave these railways the right to use these level crossings we did it in contemplation of things as they were then, and when nobody supposed that there would be the danger that has arisen since because of the acceleration of speed, the multiplication of trains and double tracking. So that, when the people say that they think the railways which created the danger should pay the cost of removing it they are not unreasonable. When they say that this danger is increased at the instance of the railways because of conditions that were not contemplated when we gave them permission to cross the highways upon the level I say they are not unreasonable. And they are equally not unreasonable when they say that the cost of protecting against this great danger should be borne by the creature which causes the danger. The danger is not in the railway running its trains slowly enough or infrequently enough, but the danger is in the multitude of trains and in the rapidity with which they are run. None of these accidents in which people are killed are caused by slowly running trains. These accidents occur because the train does not stop or slow down either because there is no station at the crossing or because it is an express train which does not stop at Mr. LANCASTER.
that point. It is the rapidity of the train that kills the people. In cities, towns and villages, but more particularly in villages and small towns, are these deaths occurring. Why? Because trains running from city to city, or from city to large town, or large town to city, run through villages and small towns at the rate of sixty miles an hour, and it is these trains that are causing the deaths and injuries. The rapidity is such that people cannot avoid the train in time. That was never contemplated when permission to cross highways was given some years ago. So that when we speak of contributing, I want it distinctly understood that in so far as I am concerned I can see no possible ground or excuse whatever for any contribution being made by the people of the state, municipalities, or provinces to render nugatory the great dangers which our railways cause while they are running upon the level crossings. That is why I say we should divide the question into these two subjects. The danger is entirely the creation of the railway because of the action of the railway in multiplying the number and increasing the rapidity of their trains. They are doing this for their own profit and properly so. We want them to make as much profit as they can, to carry as large a quantity of goods as they can and as many people, but while they are running these trains in the interest of the country they are running them for their own profit. At the same time by virtue of the carrying on of their business they create a danger upon these level crossings which was never contemplated when we gave them permission to cross them.
I have given this matter a good deal of consideration, and speaking for myself, 1 cannot see any just ground for saying that anybody other than the railways should contribute to the expense of protecting the level crossings. Of course the total abolition of level crossings is the ideal condition but as we know that is so expensive as to be prohibitive in many cases. The abolition of the level crossings, that ideal condition, would be more or less interfering with the easement which you gave to these railways when you permitted them originally to cross on the level. You said to them that in order that they might raise capital to build their railways at a moderate cost they might use the King's highways, and therefore in fairness to them-and I want to be fair to the railways-we should, I think, contribute to some extent to the cost of bringing about that ideal condition. But we would not be the only gainers by that ; the railway companies themselves will save thousands of dollars a year because it will then not be possible for them to come in contact with any obstruction on their track which would impede and endanger their trains in operation. Such a condition would

also save them an immense amount of money in maintenance, and before the special committee which some years ago considered that Bill which has now for the third time gone to the Senate, the representatives of the railway companies admitted that if they had the means they would prefer crossing under or over a highway, but the expense made it out of the question. The railways always admit that the expense of maintenance is comparatively trifling once you have the level crossing done away with and the grades separated. Therefore, when we take from them the right or the easement to run upon the level which we gave them in their original incorporation, it is worth something to the people and the people should con tribute. This question is very much allied to wl;o should contribute, and here I differ from the Minister of Railways. Why should the province or municipality pay? Has not this parliament of Canada taken under its wing all the railways of the country that are of any moment and given them to the control of the Dominion Railway Commission to the exclusion of all provincial authority. This question is very much allied to the question of subsidies to railways. We grant a subsidy to a railway to develop the country and to furnish transportation facilities, and if in doing that we find the railway ought to be constructed more expensively by eliminating level crossings, I suppose the subsidy would be increased. I am not saying that we should not in some proportion contribute to the cost of eliminating level crossings, but I can see no reason why it should come out of any other purse than the Dominion exchequer. Why should the small town or village in which these1 accidents occur be made to contribute. It is not they who get the benefit of the fast running trains; it is the larger cities. I would not agree entirely with my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) that the cities should be put on a different plane.

I did not quite say that. When I said I would leave the cities to take care of themselves I meant that the cities having a large number of able representatives in this House, they should deal with that question for themselves.

In view of that explanation I do not differ from my hon friend (Mr. Lennox) as I thought I did, but of course the cities must allow a member of this House who represents a rural constituency to give his ideas on the general question, and I quite agree with the Minister of Railways that we should approach this in a broad and general way and not from any local standpoint. And, if there is going to be any general principle laid down, what better general principle can you have than that thei state should pay. The city pays more taxes to the Dominion than the 391
village does, and why therefore not let the city through thei Dominion exchequer, and the town and the village through the Dominion exchequer contribute their share. The municipality, unless it is a large municipality, gets no benefit from these fast running trains and my contention is that unless you put the burden upon the Dominion entirely you are not going to do substantial justice. I do not think there is any question but that a very great majority of the people of this country while they would be willing to be taxed in some way for the elimination of level crossings, would, 95 per cent of them say, that there is no fairness in taxing either the province or the muni cipality for providing protection upon crossings where the trains are to continue to run upon the level. The hon. Minister of Railways says that the municipality creates the traffic. Is that quite a reason for saying that the municipality should pay the cost of protecting the level crossings? The municipality creates the traffic for the profit of the railway. The more the municipality prospers, the more goods are shipped on the railway and the more it contributes to the profits of the railway; but the municipality gets no part of the profits of the railway. The railway is making that much more profit from the people; the people are that much better customers of the railway. But the people have no opportunity to share in the profits of the railway, and of course cannot have, unless there is government ownership. If the people contribute to increase the traffic of the railway, more people are liable to cross the tracks on the highway, and therefore there is greater liability for accidents. That seems to me to be no argument for saying that the people ought to pay more for the protection of the highway. I would put it the other way, by saying that the railway ought to pay more, because it is creating more danger and because it is getting more traffic.
