I wish to say a word or two in regard to what has been done by this House on this matter. I said several years ago in this House that so long as the railways cross the highways on the rail level, they should protect the highways at their own expense. It took this House some years to come to that conclusion. Bills which I had the temerity to introduce for several years, five years ago, four years ago, three years ago, did not pass; but the combined wisdom of this House put the Bill into shape that it passed three years ago unanimously. I did not get all I contended for. I did not get the principle of protection so that the railways would have absolutely to protect and be at the mercy of a court or jury in some particular case. But this House concluded to send up to the Senate a Bill which required the Railway Commission to decide what protection should be necessary in the thickly settled parts of

cities, towns and villages, and provided that this protection should be afforded at the expense of the railway. The decision was not left to the mere whim of any jury, but was submitted to the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners, who were to decide what protection should be afforded for any particular crossing or class of crossings, and were to impose on the railway only what expense would be fairly necessary to carry out their order. Of course, that decision of this House in regard to level crossings does not touch the question of contribution to the cost of abolishing level crossings. That question, as the Minister of Railway says, has never really been dealt with by this House. The Act passed three years ago by this House and sent to the Senate would not apply to any case where there is a subway or an overhead bridge, and where the railway goes either under or over the highway. Although I am open to conviction, having no other object than the Minister of Railways, which is to eliminate this terrible evil from the country, I am bound to say that I am more than ever of the opinion that the principle adopted by this House for three years was a salutary principle; that is to say, that while the railways continue to run on the level across highways, they must put in some protection, to be determined by the Board of Railway Commissioners in every instance, and that if they do not do that, they must slow down their trains to ten miles an hour.
If we come to the conclusion that we have to eliminate level crossings, I am with the Minister of Railways that there should be some contribution. So long as we do not eliminate, I am dead against, and I believe the people of this country are dead against, any municipality or the province or the Dominion contributing in any way to the protection of level crossings by the railway, which creates the whole danger and has multiplied it greatly since it got permission to run on the highways. But when we eliminate level crossings and make the railways, as some of the states have done, remove a certain number every year, I am in favour of the people contributing a certain portion of the cost. I am not prepared to say what would be a fair proportion; we would have to go into certain calculations as to what it would cost in different parts of the country. Perhaps a fair contribution would be from 15 to 25 per cent. I am not going to commit myself to any particular proportion; but certainly it should not be over 25 per cent; and I believe the contribution should come out of the Dominion treasury, and not from the provinces or municipalities, because the Dominion has usurped the jurisdiction of the provinces with regard to railways, and has taken away from them the power to put any restrictions upon them or to control them in any way.

In conclusion, I might point out to the Minister of Railways that if these statistics of the number of deaths, which have been given to him, are correct-and I do not doubt that he believes them to be correct- I am very much surprised; 'because I have for five or six years kept track of the accidents at level crossings, and though I may have lost some, my records show fully 25 per cent more than the number of deaths shown by those statistics. My records show that, instead of 270, over 400 people were killed at level crossings during the last five years. But, assuming the figures given by the board to the minister, and no doubt believed by the board to be correct, the board has no knowledge that they represent the actual number of people killed, because it gets the information from the railways. It is true the information has to be sworn to by some officer of the company, but he does not run the trains or see the accidents. He gets his information from the reports sent in to him, and he has not the evidence of the man who knows; he has only hearsay evidence, coming through a lot of sub-officers down to the men on the trains, and the minister will readily understand that if the railways can attribute an accident to anything that will exonerate them, they will do so. Therefore, although the number of deaths may be correctly stated in their reports, the cause of death is not always given correctly. I say this because I know that the Railway Commission wants to serve the people properly, and if they will take the warning that they ought to have the statistics furnished them by the railway companies carefully looked into and not rely on them entirely, it will do no harm. The proportion, even if correctly stated by the Minister of Railways, is one to each 425 miles in Canada, while in the United States it is 1 to 660 miles, and the difference is due to the fact that the legislation in the United States is more advanced.
I shall not, in view of the discussion that has taken place, trouble the House any longer. I trust that anything that I have said will be accepted in the spirit in which it was uttered. My sole object is to assist in enacting legislation which will eliminate this terrible evil. If my Bill which has again gone to the Senate be found after a year's experience not sufficient, we shall have to try and improve on it. And as regards the elimination of level crossings, with which the Bill sent to the Senate does not deal, I shall be glad to assist the Minister of Railways in every way possible, to put into practical legislation the protection of the people. But in my opinion the contribution, if any is required to be made by the people, should not be attempted to be levied on the provinces or on the municipalities at all, but be paid entirely by the federal authorities.

I wish to preface the very few remarks I intend making on this subject, Mr. Speaker, by expressing my gratification at the unanimous concurrence of the House in the Bill of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), and I hope that, in dealing with this question of level crossings, which is recognized by members on both sides as of vast importance, we will find equal unanimity. I would not have risen at all to address you, sir, did I not consider it my duty to place the county of Frontenac right before this House. In reply to an inquiry which I had on the paper regarding the accident down near Kingston at the Montreal street crossing some time last month, the Minister of Railways made the statement that the Grand Trunk Railway showed a willingness to go on with the building of the subway, but that the county of Frontenac and the city of Kingston objected on account of the expenditure. As the hon. minister had not the opportunity to get the facts, his error was excusable, but I wish to put the position of the county of Frontenac in that matter correctly before the House. As far back as 1898, Mr. D. D. Rogers, who then represented the county in this House, took steps to have the railway crossings in the county protected. In 1902 the county sent a deputation to Ottawa which waited on the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. That deputation asked that a subway be built at the outer station near Kingston. True the city of Kingston did raise the objection that as the station was outside the city, they should not be asked to bear any part of the cost. However, the request of the county of Frontenac was granted by the Railway Committee and that commission issued an order placing the cost of the approaches on the county and city jointly and calling on the Grand Trunk Railway to proceed with the work. Nothing however was done, despite the protests of the county of Frontenac on several occasions against efforts made by the city of Kingston and by the Grand Trunk Railway system to prevent the subway from being built. Despite these protests nothing was done until February 17, 1904. The county council then sent a letter to Mr. Hayes, of the Grand Trunk Railway, asking him to go on with the work as ordered by the Railway Committee, and in June, 1904, at a special sitting of the Board of Railway Commissioners the Grand Trunk applied to have the former order of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council amended. This request was not granted, but the Board of Railway Commissioners, at the request of the council- and I want to emphasize that-approved of the order of 1902, and asked the Grand Trunk Railway to go on and construct the subway. No steps, however, were taken by the Grand Trunk Railway to build that subway or protect the public from June,
1904, to July, 1905. At that time it came to the knowledge of the county that a somewhat _ similar case was pending in which the city of Toronto was interested, and in July, 1905, the county of Frontenac expressed its willingness to allow the matter to stand until that case was finally decided. These facts clearly show a disregard by the Grand Trunk Railway of the order of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, in the first instance, and then of the subsequent order of the railway board, as well as a disregard for the public. Throughout this whole matter for the last ten years, there has been no lack of effort made by the county of Frontenac to have the subway built and certainly no effort made to prevent its construction. In spite of the opposition in the adjoining municipality of the city of Kingston and of the Grand Trunk Railway, the county of Frontenac has been continually persistent in its endeavours to have the subway constructed and the public protected.
I have here a memorial addressed to this House by the council of the county of Frontenac, calling attention to the number of accidents at that level crossing and asking this House to take such steps as will insure the protection of the public. This petition is signed by the warden of the county and every member of the county council. It has been said that since the Dominion and provincial governments have contributed by bonus or other substantial aid to the construction of this railway, they are accessories to the danger created. I cannot see the matter in that light. If we go back to the time when the Grand Trunk Railway was constructed, we can understand that the municipalities were deeply interested in having that railway built, but they had no idea that, as the years went by; the danger would become so great as it is, owing to the speed of trains and other causes. Let us take the position of the Grand Trunk Railway in this matter and I am going to confine myself almost entirely to the conditions in my own county. Let us take this crossing, popularly called the Montreal Street crossing. There have been a number of deaths at that crossing. It has been said by the Minister of Railways that a good many accidents are due to individul carelessness. I do not think that could be contended as regards deaths occurring in that place. I believe the railways should be held responsible so far, at least, as that particular crossing is concerned. And I will give my reasons: When the railway was first built, there was only one track. Later, they laid another track in the course of double-tracking their system. But, more than that, they made a railway yard or shunting ground right across the highway. I submit that when the Grand Trunk Railway laid six tracks across the highwav there, they did so with an utter disregard of the convenience of the travel-

ling public, and with a criminal disregard of the lives of the people using the highway. So far as expense in making that crossing safe is concerned, I think the responsibility should fall upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company which created the danger.
I am not going to attempt to lay out a plan whereby these dangers can be obviated. But I believe that something can be done with regard to the hundreds, perhaps thousands, of these crossings that will lessen the danger-done quickly and at comparatively little expense and without waiting for the more general action under which all crossings may be dealt with. There are many crossings in country places where the trees or bushes approach close to the railway on either side of the highway so that a person travelling on the highway cannot see the train apnroaching until he is on the track, and so cannot take means to avoid danger. I think many members of this House who have travelled through the country will agree with me that by simply cutting down the bushes or trees which obstruct the view of the people travelling on the highway, much might be done to remove danger at these level crossings. Again, I think that in laying out new towns or cities, danger might be greatly lessened by making it obligatory to build streets running parallel with the railway track into which the streets running at right angles would run. In this way the crossings could be merged into a few and danger greatly lessened, and that at comparatively little expense.
I have no intention of going into this subject on broad lines. It has been very ably introduced by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) who has contributed to the debate many facts and figures, which, I am sure, we shall all consider carefully and with great interest. My object in speaking was simply to place my own county in a proper light before this House, so far as these level crossings are concerned. The people of the county of Frontenac have hot asked what their share. of expenses would be to get rid of these level crossings. They have asked that the danger be removed. Up 'to the present time at least, there has been no cavilling on their part at the expense. I trust this matter will receive the attention of both sides of the House, and that it will be dealt with thoroughly and in a way to prevent the fatalities which we all so much deplore.

I merely wish to add a word to this very interesting discussion to express to the House the great interest that we in the province of Quebec take in the very important question raised by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). I had not the advantage of hearing all that was said by that hon. gentleman in support of his motion; but reading the motion I find that it expresses exactly our feeling upon this subject. 1 have not seen the report showing the number of Mr. EDWARDS.
accidents that have occurred, but I think that we have had, in Quebec, about the same number of these distressing fatalities as have happened in the province of Ontario -somq that we have had during the nast year being of a most arm filling character. We have not, in the past, taken as much interest in the' discussion of this subject as has been evinced by our colleagues from Ontario. Indeed, these hon. gentlemen have persistently brought this matter to the attention of the government. It is also a very urgent question for us in the province of Quebec. I was glad to hear the declarations made by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), that the government was going to take up this subject without delay and see if something could not be done to diminish the number of fatalities. I listened to what was said by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), and I quite agree with 'him that, so far as making the level crossings safe is concerned, there should be no contribution by anybody but the railway companies themselves. But when you would propose to eliminate a level crossing altogether, I must say that I feel some embarrassment in holding the same conclusion. I do not know if I understood my hon. friend to say that he thought that no contribution ought to be made except by the federal government.
Yes, I say so-as distinguished from the municipality and the province.

It may be that my hon. friend is right. He has given a great deal of study to this question, which I have not. But I incline rather to believe that not only the government should contribute, but there should be some mode by which the municipality should contribute in a proportion which I am not prepared to designate at the present moment. The elimination of level crossings by the railway company with a contribution only by the government would give rise to a great deal of difficulty, I think, because it involves interference with the roads. I think jt would be necessary-and I think it would be fair as a general rule-that the municipalities should contribute something, and that they should be interested and co-operate in the elimination. I do not think the province should be called upon to contribute-I do not see any reason why such a contribution should be called for. In Montreal at least, we have found that the urgent necessity for the elimination of these terrible death-traps arises from the growth of municipalities around the crossings, making a great artery of the road which crosses the railway, and thus making it far more dangerous. This and other reasons, I think, might be adduced as reasons why the municipality should become interested in the work and contribute in some small proportion. I think that in

Toronto the work of substituting other crossings for level crossings was contributed to by the municipality under special agreement
In Montreal we concluded an agreement with the Grand Trunk for the elimination of level crossings by contributing, I think, the sum of $1,000,000, and I would be inclined to say that not only the municipalities interested in the elimination of the crossings but also the government should contribute something. I would be inclined to place the initiation of that elimination with the municipalities. Of course any scheme of that kind would, under the present conditions, necessitate enabling legislation by the provinces empowering the municipalities to take action and to have recourse to what is in reality a Dominion tribunal established to regulate our federal railways and, having had recourse to that tribunal, to be bound by its directions. I think it is only fair in some instances I have in mind to ask that the municipalities should contribute something, and that the Dominion government should contribute a fixed proportion determined in advance, but not an arbitrary proportion, a percentage of so much which would be defined by legislation.
This motion entirely meets with the views and desires of the province of Quebec and I hope the promise made by the Minister of Railways will be fulfilled as promptly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, in supporting the very excellent resolution of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) I wish to compliment him upon the research he has made and on his very excellent speech in support of his motion. The subject is one of the mo3t important that comes before this parliament for consideration. It is associated with the subject of transportation, and transportation is, after all, the highest politics and the vital question for the parliament of Canada to consider. Anything in reference to transportation ought to be considered carefully and well by the people of Canada. It is all-important to us that the transportation of passengers and freight should be rapid in order to compete with other countries. If we have speed and level crossings we must have danger to the people of the country. The figures brought forward by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in support of his resolution giving the number of accidents which occurred among railway employees on this continent in comparison with other countries where they have better provision for safeguarding public crossings were appalling. I had no idea the death rate was so high. We are suffering from the effects of early conditions in this country. We were bound to have railways, but we could not
have them if we imposed European conditions upon them. We had to submit to all -.these difficulties and dangers which now accompany our railways in order to get them. We are getting out of that 'position now. What ought we to do? We should do as the Minister of Railways has suggested and impose upon railways to which we grant charters in future certain provisions in reference to crossings. I prefer the manner suggested by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), that these conditions should be statutory and the enforcement left either to a court or to the Railway Commission. But the time has arrived when we must do something not only in the interest of the people of the country themselves, but in the interest of the railway companies. They are anxious to have the Commission make inquiry into these .crossings for the purpose of arriving at some plan or other by which these dangers should be either gradually eliminated or in some way guarded against. The amount that a railway company pays in the shape of damages for loss of life, in pensions to injured employees and destruction of material would to a great extent offset the cost of doing away with the level crossings or guarding them. I was struck with the law of Connecticut mentioned by the hon. member providing that each railway line in the state shall eliminate one of these dangers for every 60 miles of road each year. That would be a gradual im-pfovement in the conditions.
I realize the difficulty of an arrangement between the federal and provincial governments and the municipalities as to contributions towards the elimination of these crossings. My contention is that the power vested by the British North America Act in the federal government with respect to railways covers everything incidental to the charter which we give them. If it is necessary to cross a highway, jurisdiction over which is in the province, we do not need to get legislation from that province in order to regulate the manner of crossing. The very power given to us to grant a charter for a railway gives us everything incidental to it. I am not going to give any opinion of my own, but I am going to state to the House that I have listened to the biggest lawyers that were ever in this House, to Ministers of Justice to whom the question had been submitted, and they were all of the opinion that where power was given to the federal government to do a thing everything in the slightest degree incidental to it, although the province would otherwise have had jurisdiction, was also given to the federal government. What practical legislation can we enact on this question? It would be unwise and unfair to pass legislation to say that a crossing shall be overhead or under-

ground. In Great Britain that is the law except in very exceptional cases. As my hon. friend says, a level crossing is permitted perhaps in the Highlands of Scotland. where there is not much travel over the road, and then a gate is required to protect it. We cannot adopt such a law as tl at in this country at the present time. M e could not get railways built, but we must gradually go in that direction. One of the primary objects that we must keep in view in our legislation in reference to lailways is the protection of the lives of the people, and our legislation should have that tendency as long as it does not act as a detriment or as a bar to the development of our transportation facilities. A well considered scheme may be thought out, one that would apply to the future and also have regard, to a certain extent, to the past. I prefer not giving powers to the Commission to be exercised arbitrarily as they think proper. I prefer the suggestion of my hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) that there should be a well thought out scheme adopted by the parliament of Canada and that it should then be placed in the hands of the Commissioners to be carried out. Whatever scheme is adopted its guiding principle should have in view greater protection to the public at level crossings.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext: What I say is that if the municipality and the province pay in addition to the Dominion, then the municipality is paying three times over and the province twice. The man in the munici pality pays his taxes to the province and the man in the province contributes the revenue to the Dominion.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman says may be true, but I would ask him if the municipality and the province to-day receive their share of the taxes from railways, is it not fair that the municipality and the province should bear some of the burden ?
Yes, but they should not pay three times over.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The railways are paying to the municipalities and the provinces large sums in the form of taxes, and under these circumstances it is not an unfair argument to ask that they should be required to pay something towards the elimination of these crossings. I did not intend to get into an argument with my hon. friend regarding this point. I agree that this is a big, broad question, that it should not be approached in any spirit other than in that of endeavouring to, in some way, lessen the danger, to get rid of the crossings, and it should be done in the most equitable way that can be devised by this House. If it is approached in that spirit, as it will be, then I think that some scheme will be worked out whereby the demands of the people will be satisfied. There can be no doubt about this point that a scheme cannot be formulated in a day or in a week. It is a matter that will have to be carefully considered so that justice may be done to all. This is a oues-tion that the government ought to take into consideration because it is a burning question with the people of the country. It is something that should be taken into consideration at once and it is something in regard to which some decision ought to be come to as rapidly as possible. It will not do to say that in so far as the railways are concerned they are the people to blame because the people who built the railways are simply carrying out what they are bound to carry out under their charters; that is to do the best they can for the people and to improve the service as much as the service is required to be improved. In the doing of this they are running trains; they are running faster trains and they are perhaps putting the people in the way of more danger than heretofore. But they are only doing what their charter calls on them .to do, and they are doing it in the public interest and for the service of the people of Canada.

In reference to the suggestion of the Minister of Railways that this debate should not be continued in the absence of the Minister of Finance he has been good enough to say to me that he will afford another opportunity to the gentlemen who wish to speak on this question if he does not introduce a Bill this session as he intends to do. It being six o'clock I thought I would mention that that is perfectly satisfactory to me.

Would the House permit me to offer a thought for consideration in reference to the question as to municipalities and provinces contributing for all the crossings? If whether they are in my municipality or in my province the Dominion would contribute, then when my province and my municipality get the additional benefit of having a level crossing eliminated in their borders should they not contribute something more?
Is it a benefit?

I think it is a great benefit. I have no idea at all of trying to choke off discussion, and if I produce a Bill it will give opportunity for full discussion to every person. If such a calamity should overtake me that I should not be able to introduce a Bill I assure my hon. friend that the government will see that he will have every opportunity to further discuss this resolution.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.

Thursday, February 18, 1909.
